risk_security.risk: Weather related risks
risk_security.mitigation: PNGRCS had coordinated closely with provincial government authorities and DMT to stay informed on current local conditions. Location of distribution points and care centres have been evaluated based on and ensuring safe location from any further event due to weather and erosion. Heavy rains were anticipated to result in further landslides with PNGRC staff who have avoided the landslide area as much as practicable.

risk_security.risk: Political interest because of the bi-election
risk_security.mitigation: Information have been received that there were individuals providing funding support for political gain that would help in the upcoming bi-election. PNGRCS had avoided any external partnership with individuals who may have political interests for their own gain.

risk_security.risk: Road infrastructure and access
risk_security.mitigation:
Due to the impact of the landslide and erosion in surrounding areas, there was an alternative route that was used to the affected area. PNGRCS had coordinated closely with provincial government authorities, DMT and the ICRC to remain updated on localised issues and ensure safety of all transportation of staff and volunteers along with relief items.

Local authorities and PNG Defence Force have worked on repairing the main route to the affected area and has been completed. The PNG Defence Force had initially provided support to ensure the safety of movement of all personnel and logistics to the affected population but have subsequently ceased this service.

risk_security.risk: Security risk due to ethnic clashes
risk_security.mitigation: The PNG police and defence force have no longer resided in the local area. Many actors had resorted to commercial armed security companies to escort vehicles to/from and at the CC. Ongoing ethnic tensions and disenfranchised members in the local villages have presented an ongoing challenge. The PNGRCS had dispatched CEA materials and explains the role of the PNGRCS to personnel staffing informal checkpoints. Furthermore, two car movements had commenced and close coordination with the ICRC, interlocutors, provincial government authorities and the DMT have ensured that real time information on access and any security issues had enabled informed decision making.

people_assisted: In the initial stage of the response, the entire local population that was affected were the main target of the operations. However, access had proved to be an ongoing challenge, targeted support for the vulnerable population still remains to be verified and understood. Whilst remaining to be verified, the affected population is supported by many official and unofficial actors. PNGRCS was able to manage to collect some data from the most affected population identified during the MHPSS/Psychological First Aid (PFA) sessions held within the Care Center to identify those particularly at risk and their needs. The data collected indicated about 237 households; however, further data analysis done had shown that it was likely less than 200 households (about 995 people) were the realistic affected population to be targeted. This data is based on the Capacity Vulnerability assessment that was collated by PNGRCS and is used based on the targeted intervention. Furthermore, support to vulnerable host communities’ household will also be incorporated.
main_donors: The major donors and partners of the IFRC-DREF include the Red Cross Societies and governments of Australia, Austria, Belgium, Britain, China, Czech, Canada, Denmark, German, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, Liechtenstein, Malta, Norway, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Thailand, and the Netherlands, as well as DG ECHO, Mondelez Foundation, and other corporate and private donors. The IFRC, on behalf of the National Society, would like to thank all for their generous contributions.
icrc: With a sub-delegation in Mount Hagen, the ICRC is present in the highlands, responding to the humanitarian consequences of communal violence in the Enga province. The ICRC had been coordinating well with the PNGRCS and IFRC to provide security updates and at times convoy support for the volunteers supporting the disaster response effort. In addition, at an initial stage of the operation, ICRC delivered 10 body bags owned by PNGRCS to the affected site on behalf of PNGRCS.
financial_report_description: As per the financial report, there is a variance of CHF 71,223. In the early stage of the project, the Secretariat Services budget of CHF 60,000 was developed for two surge (Operations Manager & Logistics surge) which included their salaries. However, these two roles salaries were paid by their national societies (Australia Red Cross & New Zealand Red Cross). Thus, the project was only able to expense 50 per cent of that Output code (AP122) for all the in-country expenses and partial of the budget used for the PMER surge support for the Lessons Learnt Workshop.
operation_objective:
Through the support of IFRC-DREF, the PNGRCS had aimed to reach 300 households, approximately 2,000 people, affected by the landslide. However, the operations was only able to reach 338 people through the MHPSS Story telling sessions, PGI training and Community Engagement activities which included the Vulnerability Capacity Assessment. The distribution of the HHIs will be done once the provincial administration confirms the relocation sites. This will reach 972 people that have been identified through the vulnerability assessment by PNGRCS. 

The interventions had been focused mainly on coordinating and partnering with other NGOs and government bodies to accurately identify and address the needs of the affected population. The identified needs in the initial stages were:

- Water storage containers for clean and safe water,
- Hygiene kits (especially for women and young girls),
- Psychosocial support,
- Shelter (kitchen sets for relocated households),
- Blankets (considering the cold climate in the affected region).

While the core intention of the IFRC-DREF remained largely unchanged, the budget had been adjusted, which had seen an overspend and underspend of activities due to improved procedures, access challenges, and delays to resettlement. In consideration of the logistical challenges posed by the geographical area and the complexity of the operation due to safety and security concerns, this operation was proposed to last six months.
selection_criteria:
The total targeted population was 2000 people and selection included identifying the vulnerable groups that were greatly affected:
1. Population affected by the landslide, 
2. Orphanage children (parents/parent may have been killed in landslide),
3. Women headed households,
4. People living with disability,
5. Elderly,
6. Those at increased risk of SGBV.
national_authorities: National Government has formally requested for international assistance through PNG Disaster Management Team (DMT). The Provincial Disaster Centre had taken the lead and provided coordination amongst the humanitarian partners.
partner_national_society: Currently, there are not any Partners present in the country. Australian RC had been providing remote support to this operation through funding support and technical support including a surge deployment. New Zealand RC has supported a Surge Operation Manager deployment.
event_description:
On 24 May 2024, a massive landslide engulfed villages in Yambali Ward, Maip Mulitaka Local Level Government of Lagaip-Porgera District, Enga Province, Papua New Guinea (PNG). The landslide caused extensive damage to lives, homes, and livelihoods. The destruction left an estimated 1,680 individuals displaced, with approximately 3,979 individuals affected and at risk of displacement. Furthermore, 9,952 individuals were estimated to have been directly impacted by the landslide. Immediate emergency response and long-term recovery plans were crucial to addressing the needs of these affected populations and mitigating future risks and vulnerabilities.

The landslide not only devastated Yambali Ward but also caused significant instability in the surrounding area. The soil remained highly unstable, with visible cracks indicating imminent threats to lives and properties. The landslide covered two creeks with debris and boulders, blocking waterways and increasing the likelihood of further slides.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM), in collaboration with the Enga Provincial Disaster Response Team and Site Management team, conducted a Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) assessment across all affected wards (Yambali, Pokolip, Kuandak, and Yuyango) between June and July 2024. This assessment was carried out by enumerators through field observations, focus group discussions, and key informant interviews with both affected populations and local authorities. Critical sectoral needs were identified, and the assessment highlighted ongoing risks of displacement in high-risk areas prone to further landslides and environmental hazards.

Access challenges due to land instability and security issues resulted in the affected population remaining at the Mulitaka Care Centre (CC) and within host communities longer than originally anticipated. Restricted access remained a significant challenge, as government agencies struggled to build an alternate access route due to soil erosion and instability. Further complicating the situation were checkpoints and clashes en route to and from the Mulitaka CC, following the withdrawal of security support. These factors greatly impacted the ability of the Papua New Guinea Red Cross Society (PNGRCS) to conduct assessments and address gaps where humanitarian needs were not being met.

The affected area is also known to be a high-security zone due to ongoing tribal clashes. At this stage, the response has transitioned into a recovery phase rather than an immediate emergency response due to the complex nature of the situation.

The disaster response was highly complex for several reasons, which also affected the distribution of household items (HHIs) to the affected population. Security was a major concern for PNGRCS due to continuous tribal clashes, and the safety of volunteers in the field was a top priority. PNGRCS was unable to distribute HHIs, as the plan was to wait for the affected population to resettle in their new relocation area. However, this never materialized, and the affected population remains accommodated at the Care Centre near the Mulitaka Health Centre. The distribution of HHIs will now be carried out through the Australian Red Cross (ARC)-DFAT-funded project once further information on resettlement is confirmed with the Enga Provincial Disaster Office.
event_scope:
The landslide had occurred in the early hours of the morning and destroyed a portion of the main highway and severing access to the affected village. Support for the affected population had included the provision of clean and safe drinking water, as nearby water sources were contaminated by the landslide. It was estimated that a large number of children were orphaned by the landslide, requiring the restoration of family links activities to unite children with extended family members and provide psychosocial support to those traumatised. The affected population had lost their livelihoods and, subsequently, their means of survival, as food gardens and other sources of income were destroyed.

Due to the extent of the damage and the lack of official information regarding the total population in the affected area, there is still no confirmation on the total number of deaths, as data and information are still being collated. The Enga Provincial Administration Office had been working closely with the Disaster Management Team (DMT) secretariat and other humanitarian partners on the ground, providing essential items such as food and water.

Longstanding conflicts and rivalries in the surrounding areas add an extra layer of complexity to the situation. These underlying tensions were taken into consideration during the coordination, planning, and implementation of activities in PNGRCS efforts to support the affected population.

PNG’s Defence Force had led search and rescue efforts; however, the site’s remoteness, ongoing terrain movement, and damage to access roads have prevented heavy machinery from reaching the site, stalling body recovery efforts. In close coordination with local and national authorities, the UN and other partners in the field, the PNG Defence Force engineers and heavy earth-moving equipment were mobilised to the affected area. Government authorities remained focused on clearing debris and improving access to the site; however, the debris remains unstable, posing risks to the safe conduct of the operation. Finding a suitable alternate access route has also proved challenging, with the road connecting Porgera to Lae nearing completion four months after the event.

While the exact number of fatalities is still unknown, the affected community had initially estimated that a significant number of people were missing following the landslide. The confirmed number had slowly increased over time as bodies were uncovered by the affected population, who were digging by hand to search for resources such as galvanised iron within the landslide. 

Provincial authorities had underscored the unpredictable nature of the landslide, reiterating the urgent need for geohazard assessments and services during the initial stages of the landslide event, to which the Government of Australia had offered assistance. A report was produced and presented to the Enga Provincial Disaster team and other partners involved in the humanitarian response.

Two tented evacuation sites (Care Centres) were established and were initially managed by PNG Defence Force personnel. The UN (IOM, UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA) and other development partners (World Vision, Care International) had continued to assist government authorities with disaster coordination and response efforts for residents in the Mulitaka-based Care Centre. During the first few months of the response, the Provincial Administration had prepared additional food and household (HH) supplies for distribution, bolstering the relief efforts with emergency shelter, water containers, and puri-tabs that had already been distributed. Food had remained a pressing need at the Mulitaka Care Centre, as the population lost their kitchen gardens and farm animals in the landslide. Host families have also been supporting many affected families, and an assessment of their needs is pending.

Access to the Porgera-side Care Centre remains a challenge due to accessibility issues, but it is understood that this population was evacuated for safety reasons due to land instability and has access to their homes and gardens. While both communities remain in the Care Centres or with host families, many planned recovery activities have halted pending resettlement.

The United Nations Humanitarian Coordination Team had been established in Wabag and have been supporting the Provincial Disaster Committee with response coordination. The PNG Defence Force had initially provided security escorts to ensure the safe passage of relief convoys, especially in light of an unrelated clan dispute in Tambitanis, which had caused further casualties and property damage. Many humanitarian community members are based away from the affected area due to security concerns and, as such, agencies relied on security escorts for safe passage when travelling to and from the site. However, PNG Defence Force escorts have since ceased, and agencies have begun sourcing commercial security companies to escort them to and from the Mulitaka Care Centre.

The six months operations of the Enga Landslide Response had a bit of change from the original proposal of response activities. Due to on-going security issues in the Enga province area, implementation had been very slow. The initial assessment was based on secondary data that were shared by the government of PNG and that was being used as an official figure to estimate the number of people and households were impacted by the landslide. 

The initial focus of the response was to procure Household Items (HHI) and have them distributed to the affected people. However, this took longer than expected, as the provincial government authorities were not able to resettle the affected population as indicated in their official documents. PNG Red Cross Society (PNGRCS) approach for the distribution of HHIs, was to wait till the affected population have been resettled before any distribution of HHIs can be done. As a result, to date, no distribution of HHIs have been done yet but are kept at the Western Highlands branch storage containers awaiting further advise from the Enga Provincial government. 

PNGRCS had decided to conduct another vulnerability data assessment of the affected population, to get better data for analysing and identifying the most vulnerable and affected people. Based on PNGRCS assessment, about 237 households had been impacted by the landslide. These affected families are still being accommodated at the Care Centre. The UN (IOM, UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA) and other development partners (World Vision, Care International) had continued to assist government authorities especially with distribution of HHIs and food to the affected population. 

There had been good coordination with the Provincial Disaster Center, who had taken the lead to ensure that resources are distributed equally and that there is better collaboration and partnership with the development partners who have been supporting the Landslide response.
major_coordination_mechanism:
1.  Papua New Guinea National Disaster Management Team (DMT) Coordination meeting:
- The DMT is led by UN Resident Coordinator (UN RC) Office as the Coordinating Secretariat, with PNGRC and IFRC Delegation participating in an observer role.
- Most of the meetings related to the Enga landslide had been done online, attended by all the humanitarian partners in PNG.
- DMT meetings had provided the avenue for giving important updates to the partners and also for the partners to provide any additional information that were helpful for coordination purposes.
- Situational Reports have also been circulated through emails. So far, six situational reports have been sent to the partners during the early stages of the response.
- Four Cluster Leads (Shelter, WASH, Health & Protection), upon request of DMT, had host online coordination cluster meetings and also in person meetings in Western Highlands and Enga provinces.

2. Highlands Humanitarian Hub (HHH) Coordination meeting:
- Lead by Care International PNG, the HHH is made up of humanitarian partners who are located in the highlands region of Papua New Guinea.
- The WhatsApp application group chat that was created had become an avenue for better mechanism of communication and to facilitate coordination amongst the humanitarian partners. Since the departure of the former Care International PNG Country Director, the Provincial Disaster Coordinator and DMT Secretariat have been providing the coordination in this group.
- PNGRCS Western Highlands Branch had offered their office to host the coordination meetings.
un_or_other_actor: The PNG DMT is comprised of PNG Government National Disaster Management Office, UN Agencies and international organisations. The DMT Secretariat is led by UNDP and is supported by the following cluster leads: Protection (UN Women), Shelter (IOM), WASH (World Vision) and Health (WHO).
ifrc: IFRC PNG CD maintained close coordination support and technical support to PNGRCS and had participated in all the partners meetings related to the Enga landslide. IFRC had coordinated the movement coordination meeting with other RCRC partners, ICRC (in-country) and Australian RC, New Zealand RC, Japanese RC, Korean RC, Singapore RC and so on . IFRC had also mobilised two surge deployments: Operations and Logistics, to support with the operation. PMER technical support from the AP regional office had provided support to facilitate the Lessons Learnt workshop that was held in November 2024.
risk_security_concern:
Safety and security of the staff and volunteers visiting and travelling to/from the Care Center was a high priority. Close coordination with provincial authorities was necessary for all movement into the affected area and thorough planning of distributions would be conducted.

The APRO Regional Security Unit has actively supported Country Office by providing security guidance. All field missions undertaken by IFRC personnel adhere to the current IFRC PNG security regulation and filed movement control and follow the latest health advisories. In the event that deployment of personnel to affected areas is required, an additional security clearance was required and approved by APRO Regional Security Coordinator and PNG Head of Country Delegation. 

The National Society’s security framework applies to staff and volunteers throughout the operation. For personnel under IFRC security responsibility, including surge support and integrated PNS, the existing IFRC country security framework will be applied. Rapid security assessments and analyses were conducted as needed. All IFRC staff had completed the IFRC Stay Safe 2.0 e-learning courses. NS staff and volunteers were encouraged to do the same. Staff and volunteers were also kept informed of the security status and briefed on emergency response protocols  .
title: Papua New Guinea Landslide 2024
response_strategy:
The operational strategy for the PNGRCS was designed to effectively address the immediate and evolving needs of approximately 300 households, or an estimated 2,000 people, affected by the recent landslide. This strategy is informed by a thorough assessment of the evolving situation, which included significant data and information challenges, limited access to affected areas, and prevailing security issues.

The IFRC-DREF support had procured relief items as well as had mobilized volunteers to implement activities covering the needs in shelter, WASH, health, and PGI, with PGI and CEA further mainstreamed into the thematic interventions.

The operation was planned for a duration of six months, allowing for a sustained response while considering logistical challenges and the complex security environment. The strategy was designed to be flexible, with regular reviews and adjustments based on the evolving situation and feedback from the ground. This adaptive approach had ensured that the operation remained relevant and responsive to the needs of the affected population.

The six months operations of the Enga Landslide Response had a bit of change from the original proposal of response activities. Due to on-going security issues in the Enga province area, implementation had been very slow. The initial assessment was based on secondary data that were shared by the government of PNG and that was being used as an official figure to estimate the number of people and households were impacted by the landslide. 

The initial focus of the response was to procure Household Items (HHI) and have them distributed to the affected people. However, this took longer than expected, as the provincial government authorities were not able to resettle the affected population as indicated in their official documents. PNGRCS approach for the distribution of HHIs was to wait till the affected population have been resettled before any distribution of HHIs can be done. As a result, to date, no distribution of HHIs have been done yet but are kept at the Western Highlands branch storage containers awaiting further advise from the Enga Provincial government. 

PNGRCS had decided to conduct another vulnerability data assessment of the affected population, to get better data for analysing and identifying the most vulnerable and affected people. Based on PNGRCS assessment, about 237 households had been impacted by the landslide. These affected families are still being accommodated at the Care Centre. The UN (IOM, UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA) and other development partners (World Vision, Care International) had continued to assist government authorities especially with distribution of HHIs and food to the affected population. 

There had been good coordination with the Provincial Disaster Center, who had taken the lead to ensure that resources are distributed equally and that there is better collaboration and partnership with the development partners who have been supporting the Landslide response.

Effective coordination with Movement network, including the ICRC and PNSs, as well as other NGOs and government bodies, was a cornerstone of this strategy. Leveraging the expertise and resources of these partners had enhanced the overall capacity and impact of the response.

Lessons learnt from the operations is for PNGRCS to strengthen the data collection mechanism to ensure real-time assessments. That includes adopting digital tools such as KOBO toolbox and ensure good data analysis. Better coordination of the response is another learning to ensure there is a response coordinating mechanism in place at the HQ and branch level. Trained staff and volunteers who have the capacity to response to be identified and clear roles and responsibilities are shared. 

The ARC-DFAT funded project activities are focusing on the recovery phase of the response. This  includes livelihood trainings and support and also the distribution of HHIs once the resettlement site has been identified and communicated by the provincial disaster office. 

While the current situation still is complex, the Enga Provincial Health authority has asked the partners to share with them, their health activities and interventions. As part of the sustainability of the health programme and activities, the provincial health will support in complementing the activities that partners have been implementing with the affected population. The government to take ownership of the health interventions.

national_society_actions.title: assessment
national_society_actions.description:
Botswana Red Cross Society administered a qualitative survey to 100 participants utilizing convenience sampling to understand community needs in the Francistown, Gaborone, and Mabutsane districts in light of the upcoming October general elections. The questionnaire covered various topics, including safety and security concerns, health and medical preparedness, first aid and emergency response, water and sanitation needs, support for vulnerable groups, and logistics and accessibility. Data analysis involved identifying the most common themes and the proportion of responses related to each.

The respondents most frequently mentioned health complications from high temperatures as one of the likely risks that could occur during the election period. Heat complications accounted for 60.0% of the responses.  This was followed by expressions of fear that there would be crowd control issues due to the large number of people and long waiting times to cast one’s vote at 15.0%. The respondents further expressed that there are possibilities of physical injuries due to possible fights among community members and injuries due to stampedes. However, when asked on whether there were incidents in the previous elections that required first aid, 53.3% of the respondents indicated that there were no previous incidents that they could recall. In contrast, the 46.7% that recalled incidents cited cases of fainting, strokes due to the heat, and eruption of fights. The respondents also stated that existing health concerns in their communities, such as high blood pressure, low blood, diabetes, asthma, and the spread of the influenza virus, could worsen during the elections. Community members highlighted that COVID-19 still exists, and overcrowding and lack of proper sanitation could lead to the re-emergence of COVID-19. A minority also highlighted the surge of increase in abuse of alcohol and substances during elections, which worsens the forementioned risks.  

All participants highlighted that they would benefit from having medical personnel and mobile clinics at the polling stations in anticipation of collapses from heat, existing health conditions, and physical injuries. Specifically, they indicated the need for first aid personnel. This is critical as only 24.2 % of the respondents indicated that first aid resources and medical supplies were easily accessible at polling stations. The respondents also further stated the need for community members to be trained on first aid. Regional differences were observed as all the respondents stated that there was limited or no accessibility to first aid resources from the rural Mabutsane and surrounding areas.  
In addition to the above first aid needs, the respondents indicated other areas of support to vulnerable populations during the elections by providing various amenities. As a solution to the issues of heat strokes and collapses, 25.0%% of the responses requested that drinking water be made available for voters. Standpipes exist in some polling stations but are not easily accessible due to crowding, and frequent water collection from standpipes may cause disruptions. As such, recommendations were to provide bottled water or mobile water tanks.  
Additionally, 16.3 % of the responses indicated that transportation support is paramount to ensuring that the elderly and people living with disabilities can exercise their rights, as they may sometimes live a long distance from the polling stations. The need for chairs and shade in the form of gazebos was also highlighted as necessary for these vulnerable populations.
Participants stated that, given the huge crowds, the number of toilet facilities is usually low, so portable toilets are necessary. 

The assessments findings will be used to develop the contingency plan for Botswana Red Cross Society.

needs_identified.title: protection_gender_and_inclusion
needs_identified.description:
The Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) recognizes the importance of prioritizing PGI needs to ensure that vulnerable groups such as women, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities who face a unique set of challenges are included and protected during the election period. In Botswana, women traditionally make up a significant portion of the electorate and are often disproportionately affected by social and political unrest. Women’s vulnerability to gender-based violence (GBV) increases during such times, especially in the context of political rallies, crowded polling stations, and potential confrontations between political supporters. Protecting women from harassment, violence, and intimidation was a core focus of BRCS’s election preparedness plan. Children, too, are at risk during elections, particularly if disturbances escalate into violence or if they are exposed to unsafe environments while accompanying adults to polling stations. The elderly and people with disabilities, who may already face mobility challenges, are also particularly vulnerable. 

The BRCS developed a targeted approach to address these PGI needs by prioritizing vulnerable populations in its preparedness and response efforts. Women, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities were the focus of protection efforts in Gaborone, Serowe, and Francistown. In these regions, where strong political affiliations may lead to confrontations, it is crucial that these groups are given special consideration to ensure their safety and inclusion in the electoral process.

The focus on protection, gender, and inclusion during the elections is not limited to short-term emergency response. The BRCS is also committed to ensuring that the needs of vulnerable populations are addressed in the long term. This includes advocating for policies that protect the rights of women, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities, as well as working with government agencies and NGOs to create safer, more inclusive environments.

needs_identified.title: community_engagement_and_accountability
needs_identified.description:
Community Engagement and Accountability (CEA) plays a critical role in ensuring effective disaster management and response, particularly during sensitive periods such as elections. 
One of the major gaps in community engagement during the election preparedness phase was the limited involvement of vulnerable populations in decision-making processes. Women, children, the elderly, and people living with disabilities are often disproportionately affected by both political unrest and disaster-related events, yet their voices are often under-represented in planning and decision-making. Engaging these groups early on was crucial in ensuring that their unique needs were considered and addressed during elections.

Additionally, there was a disconnect between community members and decision-makers, leading to a lack of trust in authorities and the organizations tasked with disaster preparedness and response. This was especially true in politically charged environments where mistrust of government or certain political parties could impede effective collaboration and participation. Addressing these gaps required transparent and consistent communication from the Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) and other agencies, emphasizing on impartiality and community-focused nature of the election preparedness efforts.

BRCS engaged with communities prior to the implementation of the operation to identify needs. The National Society also conducted a post-elections survey to assess the relevance and effectiveness of the operation.

needs_identified.title: health
needs_identified.description:
Health interventions were critical for densely populated areas and potential hotspots for disturbances such as Gaborone, Maun, Serowe, and Francistown to ensure that voters' health and well-being are protected in the likelihood of medical emergencies. 
A pre-election assessment conducted by the Botswana Red Cross Society highlighted the following health needs: 
•⁠  ⁠60% of survey respondents cited health complications from high temperatures as a significant risk during the elections.
•⁠  ⁠15% expressed concerns about crowd control issues due to long waiting times at polling stations.
•⁠  ⁠46.7% recalled previous incidents requiring first aid, including fainting and heat-related strokes.
The election period also coincided with extreme heat which increased risks of dehydration and heat exhaustion. This necessitated the National Society's intervention to distribute water to voters. 
While pre-election assessments signaled the possibility of injuries due to political violence in politically charged areas, this possibility did not materialize. There was a peaceful transition from the old administration to the new administration which reduced the need for first aid services. This peaceful transition was a demonstration of the political stability and resilience of Botswana. 
However, preparation for the worst-case scenario was essential to ensure that there was sufficient capacity to address immediate health concerns that could arise. 

303 volunteers (241 female, 62 male) and 39 staff (21 female, 18 male) were trained in first aid for this operation with some of the trainees receiving refresher training while others received training for the first time.

planned_interventions.lessons_learnt: • Early and inclusive community engagement is critical in electoral preparedness. Sensitization efforts on voter rights and the electoral process proved effective in clarifying misconceptions and increasing awareness among community members. However, to maximize impact, such initiatives should be initiated well in advance of election periods. Additionally, extending training on inclusion and protection principles to election officials is essential to ensure a coordinated and rights-based approach throughout the electoral process. This dual focus strengthens both community understanding at both community, institutional and NS level, reinforcing from all parties the humanitarian principles and accountability.
planned_interventions.narrative_description_of_achievements:
Prior to the implementation of any initiative, the Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) ensures that all involved staff and volunteers receive mandatory training on the Code of Conduct, the Prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) Policy, and the Child Protection Policy. These trainings are essential in reinforcing the core principles and values of the BRCS.
Additional key trainings and debriefing sessions were also conducted, including sessions on Protection, Gender, and Inclusion (PGI) and Psychological First Aid (PFA), reaching a total of 342 BRCS staff and volunteers. For some participants, these were refresher sessions, while for others, it was their first exposure to such content. The trainings emphasized the importance of safeguarding and including vulnerable groups particularly women, children, the elderly, and persons with disabilities throughout the operation.

On election day, BRCS volunteers, in collaboration with presiding and electoral officers, were granted the opportunity to address voters at polling stations. They advocated for vulnerable individuals such as the elderly, persons with disabilities, and pregnant or lactating women to be allowed to skip queues. This initiative significantly improved the voting experience for over 1,500 individuals who benefited from expedited access.
Due to the public nature of the intervention and prior community sensitization, it was not possible to capture sex-disaggregated data of those who skipped queues. However, based on national records, of the 1,038,275 registered voters, 845,394 individuals participated in the election, representing a voter turnout rate of 81.4%.

The BRCS engaged with 321 (167 female, 154 male)  stakeholders across the health, safety and security, district administration, community leadership, and psychosocial services to ensure that voters receive comprehensive and appropriate services even if they are beyond the scope of the BRCS as the first medical responder. These engaged stakeholders are part of existing referral pathways across 2 thematic areas (for SGBV response and emergency medical services) in the 17 villages covered by the response. Volunteers who are well-versed in their community context and services were also reminded of these referral pathways, and 34 people were successfully referred for additional services.

However, the sensitization sessions proved effective, as some individuals were able to independently access appropriate services based on the information provided. This outcome aligns with BRCS's objective of empowering communities to seek support autonomously and effective dissemination of available referral pathways, even when referrals are not made directly by staff or volunteers.

planned_interventions.lessons_learnt:
• Effective volunteer deployment in electoral operations requires early and extensive coordination with stakeholders at all levels. The role of the National Society should be clearly communicated to both the public and polling officials at least two months prior to the elections. Early engagement helps foster collaboration, clarify mandates, and reduce public misconceptions or speculation about the National Society’s presence and activities during the electoral process.
• Clear communication about the mandate and limitations of the National Society is essential to managing public expectations and fostering trust. Misconceptions around BRCS’s role—such as expecting volunteers to dispense medication—and instances of perceived political affiliation contributed to confusion and reduced community confidence. Proactive public sensitization and transparent engagement strategies are critical to reinforcing the auxiliary role of the Red Cross, maintaining neutrality, and building stronger community trust and ownership.
planned_interventions.narrative_description_of_achievements:
• The pre-election training included a component on Community Engagement and Accountability with 39 staff and 303 volunteers equipped with knowledge on CEA principles and practices, and skills to effectively engage communities and ensure their voices are heard. At the district level and polling station level, 321 (167 female, 154 male) stakeholders were engaged, consisting of District Health Management Teams (DHMTs) personnel, Police Officers, residing Officers, Returning Officers, community leadership structures, and international and local electoral observers, amongst others, this was to ensure all departments are prepared for elections and contingency plans are being developed jointly. 
• BRCS conducted election preparedness awareness as they conducted some community assessments to understand community needs in the Francistown, Gaborone, and Mabutsane districts in light of the October 2024 General Elections. The qualitative study covered various topics, including safety and security concerns, health and medical preparedness, first aid and emergency response, water and sanitation needs, support for vulnerable groups, and logistics and accessibility. The respondents most frequently mentioned health complications from high temperatures as one of the likely risks that could occur during the election period. Utilizing these findings, the BRCS incorporated water distribution into its response plan as well as provision of gazebos for shade at selected polling stations. 
• To ensure that the mandate of the BRCS and role during elections was well understood by the general public, the Secretary General of the BRCS conducted 1 TV and 2 Radio interviews as part of community discussions. The National Society also released statements to the press on the same. The readership of one of the newspapers in which the press release was published was 150,000. The initial plan did not involve media engagement, however, there was a negative article from a local newspaper (Mmegi) that required the National Society to engage with the public through mass media to clarify the BRCS role and mandate. 
• Post the election, the National Society conducted a participatory exit survey to assess the relevance and results of the support provided during the election period. The findings aim to inform future programming, improve service delivery, and meet community needs. At least 49% of the survey participants reported that they were aware of what the Botswana Red Cross was doing in their community. Similarly, this proportion of the sample was aware of the populations being targeted for BRCS election interventions. Vulnerable populations such as people living with disabilities, pregnant women, elderly, and people living with pre-existing medical conditions such as hypertension were given priority. In overall, 52% of the respondents felt that their opinions were taken into account from the program design right to the implementation, they also reported that they were informed of how they can contact or provide feedback on the work of the BRCS in their community.
• Community engagement was well executed during the election preparedness initiative as different stakeholders were engaged from the project design to the endline survey.

This miscommunication caused delays in the BRCS first aiders assuming their positions at the polling stations. A letter from the IEC on BRCS role was shared with the Presiding Officers.

planned_interventions.narrative_description_of_achievements:
To evaluate the impact of its electoral support operation, the Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) conducted a post-election survey, mobilizing 342 personnel nationwide comprising 39 staff and 303 volunteers. The objective was to assess the relevance and effectiveness of the assistance provided during the election period. Findings from the survey are intended to inform future programming, enhance service delivery, and ensure that community needs are more effectively met.

Specific objectives of the post-election survey were to:
-Assess community awareness of BRCS activities during the elections, including outreach and feedback mechanisms.
-Measure satisfaction with the conduct, responsiveness, and professionalism of BRCS staff and volunteers.
-Identify the key challenges experienced by communities on election day and gather actionable recommendations for improvement.
The survey employed a standardized questionnaire to capture data on community awareness, satisfaction with services received, and operational or logistical challenges faced by voters. Data collection took place from 25 to 28 December 2024 in five villages—Palapye, Gaborone, Serowe, Maun, and Francistown, where BRCS had provided electoral support services. The timing of the survey posed some limitations, as many community members were either traveling or otherwise occupied during the holiday period, which affected participation rates.
A convenience sampling approach was used, with community volunteers selecting respondents residing near polling stations where BRCS had been active. Of the total respondents, 61% were women, indicating strong female representation in the feedback sample.
The key survey findings are as follows:
1. Awareness of Red Cross Activities
49% of the respondents reported that they were aware of what the Botswana Red cross was doing in their community. Similarly, this proportion of the sample was aware of the populations being targeted for BRCS election interventions. Vulnerable populations such as people living with disabilities, pregnant women, elderly and people living with pre-existing medical conditions such as hypertension were given first priority. 52% of the respondents also reported that they were informed of how they can contact or provide feedback on the work of the BRCS in their community. 
 
2. Assistance Received
28% of the respondents reported receiving direct assistance while 57% reported that a family member or acquaintance received support while 15 % indicated they were not beneficiaries of Red Cross services during the election exercise. The respondents further elaborated that of the assistance provided 9.8% was first aid, 6.6% was psychological first aid and 83.6% was water provision. 
 
3. Satisfaction Levels
Respondents who received the assistance themselves rated their overall satisfaction with BRCS support.  A majority 64.7% of the respondents were satisfied with BRCS support while 11.8% were neutral towards the support. No dissatisfaction was reported. 
 
4. Challenges Identified
The top three challenges that the respondents encountered on election day were long queues and waiting times with 42 of the 61 respondents mentioning this as a challenge. In second place was limited or lack of shaded areas. Crowd control issues were also frequently mentioned as an issue. 

5. Recommendations
Respondents were asked to suggest solutions to the challenges they encountered during election day and how the BRCS could improve its assistance in the next general election. The following were recommendations provided by the community members: 
- Ensure adequate shade is available through the provision of additional tents and gazebos. 
- Provision of an adequate number of toilets in line with the registered voters in the polling station. 
- Provision of water through water tanks or chilled bottled water. 
- Deployment of Election officers specifically for queue management.
- Mandate each polling station to have separate queues for senior citizens, disabled individuals, and expecting mothers.
- Increase number of signboards to guide voters.
-Use of public addressing systems to ensure high level of community awareness on BRCS election support. 
- Ensure that accessibility aids such as ramps and special toilets suitable for people with disabilities are provided.

Volunteers trained on PFA will be deployed at polling stations and high-tension areas, offering support to voters, election staff, and community members. In cases of severe trauma, individuals will be referred to mental health professionals.

planned_interventions.lessons_learnt:
• The use of mobile health trucks, particularly for non-communicable disease (NCD) screening, could have enhanced community health outreach by leveraging the high turnout at the polling stations. Future operations should consider integrating such services to maximize the humanitarian impact during large public gatherings like elections.
• Analyzing trends in voter turnout times, demographic patterns, and weather conditions can significantly enhance operational planning. Such data should be used to inform resource allocation—particularly for critical supplies like water—to ensure timely and equitable distribution, reduce stress on volunteers, and better respond to the needs of vulnerable groups during peak voting periods.
• Providing additional tents and seating at polling stations can significantly improve voter comfort, particularly in open or high-traffic areas. Ensuring adequate shelter and rest areas contributes to a more dignified voting experience and helps prevent fatigue or discomfort, especially for the elderly, persons with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups. The logistic and basic facilities challenges must be tackled for these groups.
planned_interventions.narrative_description_of_achievements:
BRCS conducted trainings for its 342 BRCS staff, and volunteers that were deployed for the Election Readiness Initiative, on Psychological First Aid (PFA) and Emergency First Aid, for others this was a refresher training but for some it was their first training. These trainings aimed to prepare them to support individuals with election-related stress, trauma, and any anticipated injuries. For severe cases, the individuals were referred to professionals. 

Elections can be unpredictable, and having first aid kits on hand ensured that immediate medical attention was available for all injuries or health emergencies. This preparedness helped to manage minor injuries and prevent them from becoming more serious, as such, 275 first aid kits were procured to support not just the communities but the poll workers and volunteers too who were on the front line during the elections, working long hours under stressful conditions. First aid kits provided them with the necessary supplies to address any health issues, ensuring their well-being and ability to continue their duties
The first aiders responded to 78 cases of medical need, which were emanating from the hot weather conditions and complications from existing medical conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure. Due to high temperatures of 35 degrees to 38 degrees, 35% of the cases attended to were dehydration cases, in which the first aiders ensured fluid replacement and appropriate body positioning under shade. The second most type of medical need attended was physical injuries of which some were caused by falling down as the voters were navigating queues, as well as encounters with environmental hazards such as fallen tree branches. The cases in the ‘other’ category included allergy reactions, previous surgery, reacting to long queuing times, hunger, and drunkenness. 
 53 voters (42 female, 11 male) were provided with PFA to alleviate emotional distress. The reasons for emotional distress as reported by the assisted voters were mainly complaints regarding long queues which impacted their schedules e.g. some voters had left their children at home and needed to return quickly, and anxiety or fear of crowds. 

• Distribution of water: With the support of 303 volunteers, the BRCS team reached 41,092 people through the distribution of 41,092 bottles of water (500ml) which amounted to 20,546 liters of water during the election day. This support was critical due to the high temperatures experienced during the day. Support offered by BRCS, also continued 8 November 2024 during the inauguration of the president where the BRCS distributed a further 384 water bottles (192 litres) to the public. 
The first aid was done upon request and on a need basis, therefor first aiders provided support to 153 people of which 78 received basic first aid, 53 psychological first aid, and referral support to 22 people. Of the 153 voters directly assisted, 111 were female while 42 were male which corresponded with the statistics that Botswana’s voters were predominately female. At least 45% of the voters were persons with special needs including elderly voters aged 65 years and above, people living with disabilities, pregnant women, and children under the age of 5 years.

In many cases, there was only one toilet available per location, which was insufficient given the number of voters. The lack of adequate sanitation, hygiene facilities, shade, and seating contributed to voter discomfort and led to minor tensions and complaints from the public.
•  Inability to meet water demand as most polling stations ran out of water. Limited water supplies meant that volunteers prioritized distributing water to individuals most in need.

people_assisted:
This operation prioritized vulnerable populations, specifically targeting the elderly, women, children, people with disabilities, and individuals living in poor conditions, through engagements with volunteers and community leaders as they live in the same communities. 
Out of the 74,205 targeted people, the people in need are 59,364, with 54% being women, 49% men, 32% being youth and 3% being people with disabilities.

Through the adjusted communication on NS mandates and principles, NS engaged with mass media agencies such as radio, TV to ensure the key messages were scaled-up to the maximum population. This adjustment in the strategy was to mitigate any rumors, misconceptions and perception issues raised from the misquoting of NS plan by one of the local media. This initiative scaled-up the reach of the NS to 150,000 people. 

This focus on Mashonaland West follows the specific trnd of the malaria there. However, the NS has also ensure an analysis is being done on how to leverage the resources available in country on the WASH and Health interventions associated to water related diseases. While this Malaria DREF is focused specifically on Mashonaland West, the ongoing Cholera DREF operation (MDRZW024) targets distinct and non-overlapping locations—namely Beitbridge, Bindura, Hwedza, Uzumba-Maramba-Pfungwe (UMP), as well as areas within Mashonaland Central and East. This clear geographic separation ensures that there is no duplication of efforts between the two operations. Instead, for WASH, health awareness, and sanitation-related interventions under the respective operations, the activities are complementary. Each operation is designed based on specific health risks, epidemiological patterns, and community needs in their respective areas. As such, while there may be thematic overlap (e.g., health promotion), the interventions reinforce each other rather than duplicate, enabling a coordinated and context-specific public health response across different regions.

operation_objective:
The overall objective of this operation was to ensure the safety and well-being of communities during Botswana's General Elections from September to October 2024 by providing essential first aid and mental health support, while fostering community engagement and communication to address potential challenges.

The NS conducted risk assessments in the hotspots of political unrest, particularly the major cities and towns. The target group of 74,205 people was identified as 10% of the most at risk communities in all three districts. In this group, 59,364 people were identified as the number of people who were most in need. The NS used a three-phase strategy focusing on pre-election, during election and post-election. The strategy was as follows:

o	Pre-Election (September-October):  Trained volunteers on first aid, psychological first aid, and crowd management. Pre-positioned first aid kits and ambulances at polling stations in Gaborone, Serowe, and Francistown. Conducted community engagement activities to inform the public of BRCS’ mandate and services.

o	During Election (30th October): Deployed volunteers to key polling stations with first aid kits. Volunteers monitored the situation and provided on-the-ground support, including first aid and psychological assistance for any election-related injuries or trauma.

o	Post-Election (November): Continued monitoring for protests or disturbances after results were announced. Volunteers were on standby for rapid deployment to areas of unrest.
selection_criteria: These groups are often the most affected during times of political instability, particularly during elections, due to their limited ability to protect themselves or access essential services. The elderly were a key focus because they often have limited mobility and are more susceptible to health issues during emergencies. Their ability to access medical care or evacuate in times of unrest is typically hindered, making them a high-priority group for medical assistance, including first aid and transportation. Women and children were also critical targets due to their increased risk of violence, especially in conflict-prone situations like election-related disturbances.
national_authorities: Botswana Red Cross Society cooperated with the Independent Electoral Commission through an existing Memorandum of Understanding. An Emergency Operations Center (EOC) was activated to facilitate and coordinate real-time information sharing within the BRCS.
partner_national_society: There are no Participating National Societies in the country.
anticipatory_actions:
Botswana's 2024 elections are set against a backdrop of political tensions, economic uncertainty, and social inequality. While historically celebrated for its strong democratic institutions and steady economic growth, recent developments suggest the country is at a critical juncture. The dominance of the ruling Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) and the economic reliance on diamond revenue have led to rising political challenges and economic vulnerabilities, particularly highlighted by factionalism within the BDP, fragmentation of the opposition parties and declining demand for natural diamonds.

The North-West has established itself as a stronghold for opposition parties more especially Botswana Congress Party since 2014, and opposition won the parliamentary seats for 2019 elections  in this region with BCP under Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC), and the 2024 general elections are anticipated to be more interesting  in the sense that BPC separated from the  Umbrella For Democratic Change due to feuds among the BCP and BNF leaderships as the two parties were part of the UDC. Cities and areas where opposition parties are gaining ground, particularly in regions like the Central District and North-West, may experience heightened political tension, especially given the ongoing voter registration controversies. These regions could be classified as high-risk areas in terms of potential electoral disputes or unrest. In contrast, traditionally UDC and BDP strong areas like Gaborone may also face high or Medium risk, as this will  be impacted by the broader political struggles, especially in light of the Ian Khama-Mokgweetsi Masisi feud and the political rivalry of the two parties.

Goodhope-Mmathete Constituency is one of the potential hotspots for social unrest following the decision of the ruling Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) central committee on September 23rd 2024 to remove him as parliamentary candidate for Goodhope-Mathethe constituency. Dr Edwin Dikoloti who is the former Health Minister, has made an urgent application before the Gaborone HIGH court. He is challenging the decision of the BDP central commitee to replace him with Peggy Serame, the current Minister of Finance, who he defeated in the party primary elections. Dikoloti has since registered as an independent candidate under the slogan 'Wena Beulah' ahead of the 2024 General Election. He was also fired as the Minister of Health on 27.09.2024 which led to him resigning as a member of the BDP.

Moreover, the voter registration process has already been marred by controversy, with opposition parties accusing the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) of lacking transparency for not publicising the voters' roll. This issue is particularly critical as it influences public confidence in the election process, further supporting the need for a timeline of events to ensure clarity. 

Voter Registration Period: The voter registration process began on January 5th 2024  and ended on February 3rd, 2024. However, due to the low number of people registered for the 2024 elections, a supplementary registration period was extended from February 26th to March 15th, 2024. The opposition parties scrutinised the exclusion of Madibelatlhopo (a UDC observer group aimed at monitoring elections for fairness at registration stations). According to a Mmegi online report titled "Madibelatlhopo to monitor registration 'from a distance", the observer group was said to be defying the Court of Appeal (CoA)'s ruling.

The potential for disturbances and conflicts between supporters of the Botswana Patriotic Front (BPF) and the Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) presents significant challenges to the safety and well-being of citizens. The ruling BDP is also under pressure from a fragmented opposition, primarily the Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC), Botswana Congress Party (BCP) and the Botswana Patriotic Front (BPF).

Recent developments have heightened concerns about social stability, with economic issues such as inflation, high unemployment, and income inequality contributing to public dissatisfaction. Additionally, the rivalry between President Masisi and former President Ian Khama, who supports the BPF, could further escalate tensions.

Despite these challenges, analysts predict that the BDP is likely to retain power due to the opposition's difficulties in unifying effectively.

The Botswana Red Cross Society conducted risk assessments in the hotspots of political unrest, particularly the major cities and towns, in order to evaluate the current political situation, the needs of the vulnerable communities and to gain an understanding of the perceptions at community level. 
The survey findings underscore significant health risks during the election period, primarily heat-related complications (60.0% of responses). Concerns about crowd control and physical injuries were also noted, with 15.0% fearing crowd-related issues. Despite 53.3% recalling no prior incidents needing first aid, those who did mentioned fainting and heat strokes. Respondents called for medical personnel and mobile clinics at polling stations, highlighting the need for accessible first aid resources. Additional requests included drinking water, and support for vulnerable populations, emphasizing the urgency for enhanced health services during elections.

As political tensions rise and the risk of election-related unrest increases, proactive resource mobilization is essential to ensure that necessary first aid and psychological first aid services are available for rapid response to emergencies. The urgency to act arises from the heightened risk of clashes between BPF and BDP supporters. Both parties have substantial followings, and as elections approach, the intensity of their campaigns is expected to increase. Although Botswana's electoral processes are generally peaceful, history indicates that protests can occur, particularly in politically divided areas. If tensions escalate, risks of physical injuries, stampedes, and general unrest could emerge, underscoring the need for immediate intervention. 

Election periods also present unique health risks that require early preparation. One major concern is the long queues voters often face, particularly in hot weather, which can lead to dehydration, heatstroke, or heat exhaustion, especially among the elderly, individuals with pre-existing health conditions, and pregnant women. With elections scheduled for October, the warm weather in Botswana may exacerbate these health risks. Without adequate preparation, incidents of fainting and fatigue could overwhelm local health services.

Another significant health concern during elections is low blood sugar (hypoglycemia). Voters, particularly those with diabetes, may struggle to manage their symptoms while waiting in long lines without access to food. Without snacks or quick energy sources, individuals may experience dizziness, confusion, and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness. The BRCS can play a vital role in addressing these issues by ensuring that trained volunteers are present at polling stations with first aid kits that include glucose tablets, water, and other essential supplies.
event_description:
Botswana held its 13th General Elections on October 30, 2024, which determined the composition of the 13th National Assembly and 5th President of Botswana.  The key political contenders included the former ruling Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) and the primary opposition parties: the Botswana Patriotic Front (BPF), the Botswana Congress Party (BCP), and the Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC). The UDC garnered a historic win out seating the former ruling party. This transition to the new regime was peaceful despite the atmosphere of controversy and instability that was experienced in the leading up to the elections. 

These elections took place amidst significant controversy, largely due to tensions between former President Ian Khama and President, Mokgweetsi Masisi. This political rivalry created an atmosphere of instability in the lead-up to 30 October 2024. Key history developments and major events that contributed to the 2024 socio-political troubles:
1. April 1, 2018: Mokgweetsi Masisi succeeds Ian Khama as President of Botswana.
2. May 2018: Khama begins openly criticizing Masisi’s leadership, particularly the dismissal of Isaac Kgosi, the former Director of Intelligence and Security Services (DISS).
3. June 2018: Khama intensifies his criticism, focusing on Masisi's decision to lift the elephant hunting ban and his general governance style.
4. December 2018: Khama resigns from the BDP, citing irreconcilable differences with Masisi.
5. May 2019: Khama forms the Botswana Patriotic Front (BPF) to challenge the BDP in the elections.
6. October 2019: The BDP wins the elections, though the BPF makes notable gains, particularly in Khama's home region of Serowe.
7. November 2019: Khama leaves Botswana, initially claiming it was for a vacation but later citing concerns for his safety.
8. May 2022: Khama confirms he is living in self-imposed exile in South Africa due to fears of political persecution by the Masisi administration.

In 2024, additional tensions arose between the Umbrella for Democratic Change (UDC) and the Botswana Congress Party (BCP), resulting in a split that has further fragmented the opposition. This division highlights the fragile nature of opposition coalitions in Botswana and suggests a potentially contentious electoral landscape.
1. September 6, 2024: Opposition legislators walk out of Parliament during a vote on the Constitutional Amendment Bill, in protest against the ruling party.
2. September 6, 2024: Clashes occur between police and protesters outside Botswana's National Assembly in Gaborone, as Parliament votes on a bill granting the president increased powers to appoint key civil servants.
4. September 13, 2024: Khama appears in court in Gaborone to seek the dismissal of arrest warrants issued in December 2021.
5. September 20, 2024: Khama returns to Botswana, with a court appearance scheduled for September 23, 2024, to face multiple charges.
event_scope:
The political atmosphere surrounding the 2024 General Elections in Botswana presented challenges that prompted the Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) to mobilize resources to augment government efforts in elections preparedness. There were concerns about potential disturbances and violence, particularly in densely populated areas such as Gaborone, Serowe, and Francistown, which have strong party support bases. The scope of potential disturbances included physical altercations between opposing political factions, protests, demonstrations, and localized violence in areas where tensions are highest. Gaborone, Maun, Serowe, and Francistown were of particular concern due to their large populations and their historical association with political activism. Goodhope-Mathethe Constituency was another potential hotspot for social unrest based on disagreements on nominations of the ruling party’s parliamentary candidates. 

In addition to the risk of injuries from disturbances, there are other health risks associated with elections in Botswana especially since high temperatures are usually experienced during the month of October. Long queues at polling stations, often in extreme heat, present a danger of dehydration, heat exhaustion, and heatstroke. Many voters, especially the elderly, people with disabilities, and those with pre-existing conditions, may struggle with standing in line for long periods without adequate access to water, food, or shade. 

In light of these possible emergencies, the Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) mobilized funds through the DREF mechanism to ensure emergency preparedness and execute its auxiliary role during the 2024 General Elections for safe and peaceful elections. Through its existing memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC), the National Society engaged in consultative meetings with the IEC to coordinate on the areas of collaboration and the selection of constituencies where the BRCS staff and volunteers would be stationed. 

24 constituencies were selected covering 157 polling stations in 17 villages being Gaborone, Mogoditshane, Goodhope, Mathethe, Mabule, Molepolole, Francistown, Tati-Siding, Butale, Senyawe, Jackalas 1, Ramokgwebana, Masunga, Maun, Palapye, Serowe, and Selibe-Phikwe. 

Across these locations BRCS’s involvement was centered around three main areas:
1. First Aid Services: BRCS stationed trained first aid personnel at polling stations and strategic points to respond to any health emergencies, such as fainting, heat exhaustion, or minor injuries. 
2. Psychosocial First Aid (PFA): BRCS staff and volunteers provided psychosocial support to individuals feeling overwhelmed to ensure their calm and emotional well-being. 
3. Provision of water: BRCS distributed bottled water at polling stations and voting centers to ensure that people remain hydrated. 

In the post election and following the closure of polling stations, the presiding officers, returning officers, party representatives, and observers congregated at selected polling stations for ballot counting of parliamentary and council seats. BRCS continued its first aid coverage during this counting process which continued to the 1st of November in areas such as Palapye, and Goodhope-Mathethe.  The post-election support offered by the National Society, also continued on 8 November 2024 during the inauguration of the president. 

This support was conducted through deployment of 303 volunteers (241 female, 62 male) and 39 staff (21 female, 18 male) with coordination from the National Society’s Emergency Operation Centre.  The National Society had also procured 275 first aid kits and visibility materials to support the identification of National Society staff and volunteers, including regalia, banners, and gazebos. BRCS ensured that the colour of the visibility materials did not coincide with any political party colours to assure the public of the society’s neutrality. Videographers were also engaged to document the National Society’s participation in the electoral process, covering the pre-election and election-day activities. Additional support from BRCS included 17 vehicles from the National Society which consisted of 2 mobile trucks.
major_coordination_mechanism:
The Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) activated its Disaster Response Team and Emergency Operations Centre (EOC) to ensure effective coordination and operational efficiency. The EOC was vital for maintaining preparedness, facilitating coordination, sharing information, and enabling timely decision-making. All team members underwent training in emergency management to enhance their capabilities.

BRCS adhered to the Safer Access Framework throughout both the pre-election and post-election phases. Staff and volunteers complied with established safety protocols and operational standards, ensuring that the BRCS can effectively respond to any emergencies that may arise during this critical period.
un_or_other_actor: No UN or other actors were engaged on this operation.
ifrc:
The IFRC provided technical support to the National Society for resource mobilization and implementation of the operation. 
2 Officers were trained on DREF applications and procedures. 

In preparations for the operation, the IFRC also conducted Election Security Contingency Planning Workshop with the NS. This planning workshop was on the Election readiness. It brought 31 staff (18 female, 13 male) and 20 (12 female, 8 male) volunteers. The objectives of the workshop were to strengthen the knowledge of staff on the Safe Access Framework which outlines strategies for increasing acceptance, security and access to communities in need.  Key areas of discussion included safeguarding the use of the BRCS emblem and upholding the 7 principles of the Red Cross movement of humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, universality and unity. Further discussions involved conducting security risk assessments and developing a shared understanding of acceptable code of conduct during elections.
risk_security_concern:
With large gatherings expected at polling stations, there are significant concerns about crowd control. 15% of survey respondents from an assessment conducted by Botswana Red Cross Society, expressed fears regarding long waiting times and crowd management, which could lead to chaos and injuries, especially if political disputes arise.
In preparations for the operation, Botswana Red Cross Society appointed a Security focal person who will liaise with IFRC Cluster Security Manager to facilitate real time exchange of information. The efforts are intended to prioritize safety of staff and volunteers.
title: Botswana General Elections 2024 - Readiness
response_strategy:
The Botswana Red Cross Society (BRCS) implemented a comprehensive response plan, prioritizing the provision of first aid, medical support, and emergency preparedness. The strategy focused on providing services to 17 villages with large populations and potential for heightened political tensions. The selected areas historically exhibited strong support of specific political parties, raising concerns about possible unrest during and after the election process. BRCS approach emphasized inclusivity and prioritization of the needs of women, children, the elderly, and people living with disabilities, while ensuring that communities with inadequate infrastructure and services are not overlooked.

A key element of the strategy was allocation of resources to cover 10% of the population in high-risk areas including Gaborone, Serowe, Maun and Francistown , focusing primarily on the most vulnerable members of society. The BRCS aimed to support residents living in poor conditions, particularly in informal settlements where access to essential services such as healthcare, clean water, and sanitation is limited. These communities are often the hardest hit during periods of instability and providing them with immediate assistance will help mitigate the impact of election-related disturbances.
As part of its preparedness plan, BRCS deployed the following resources:  

1.	275 First Aid Kits: These were distributed among volunteers in strategic locations to provide immediate medical assistance in the event of injuries. Each kit was fully stocked with essential supplies such as bandages, antiseptics, and splints.

2.	Two mobile clinics: These were stationed in Gaborone to provide emergency transport for critical cases. These ambulances will be equipped with advanced life-saving equipment and staffed with trained paramedics.

3.	Trained volunteers: BRCS surpassed its target to train 275 volunteers as 303 volunteers were trained. These volunteers underwent first aid training and disaster response simulations to ensure that they are well-prepared for the unique challenges that may arise during the election period. The volunteers were deployed in teams of two or three across the 157 polling stations, ensuring rapid response to any emergencies.

BRCS prioritized support for women, children, the elderly, and people with disabilities.
